title: From Serum to Dairy: Target Accessibility, Biointerface Engineering, and Translation Readiness in IGF-1 Biosensing
Photocrosslinked gelatin hydrogel-mediated IGF-1 delivery promotes early cartilage-like tissue formation in a rabbit auricular defect model
authors: Toshihiro Kushibiki; Yoshine Mayumi; Eiko Nakayama; Toshifumi Yamashiro; Ryuichi Azuma; Miya Ishihara
abstract: Abstract Auricular cartilage has a limited capacity for self-repair. Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) promotes chondrocyte proliferation and extracellular matrix synthesis; however, its therapeutic efficacy is constrained by rapid diffusion and a short in vivo half-life. In this study, we investigated whether IGF-1 delivered in a previously developed visible-light photocrosslinked gelatin hydrogel could promote cartilage repair. In a mouse subcutaneous model, ex vivo fluorescence imaging over 14 days showed that the hydrogel prolonged the local retention of fluorescently labeled IGF-1 compared with IGF-1 solution. In a rabbit auricular-cartilage defect model, defects were treated with saline, IGF-1 solution, hydrogel alone, or IGF-1-loaded hydrogel ( n = 5 per group) and evaluated 1 month later. The IGF-1-loaded hydrogel group formed cartilage-like tissue with rounded cells within lacunae, proteoglycan-rich matrix, and type-II collagen, which occupied 83.8% of the defect length compared with 6.4% in the hydrogel-only group. This group also showed higher COL2A1 , ACAN , SOX9 , and COL1A1 expression, more Ki-67-positive cells, and increased peripheral angiogenesis, without calcification. IGF-1 delivery using photocrosslinked gelatin hydrogels, which prolonged local IGF-1 retention, is thus a promising strategy for promoting early cartilage-like tissue formation, although long-term maturation and mechanical function remain to be established.
